title: Settlement
description: A place people live, at the scale between a region and a point of interest. What a player can walk into is a `field_map` or a `poi`; this is the thing those refer back to.

aliases.description: Other names this has been known by. Added when `Dwarka` became `North Dwarka`: canon held one Dwarka and then held several, and a rename that drops the old name breaks every reference written before it.

epoch_founded.description: An epoch id. Checked by the epoch pass, which matches any field whose *name* mentions an epoch -- this one is why that rule is written the way it is.

canon.description: How firmly this is established. `primary` is stated by the source material, `inferred` is a reading canon has committed to.

within.description:
What contains this place -- another place, a region, a settlement or a field map.

Exists because canon names far more places than it can survey. Seventeen were named by events and drawn nowhere, because only the ones legible on `dump/Partial_map.png` ever got coordinates and everything authored since has had none. Each era's chapter mentioned places the era's map did not show.

Plotting each by hand does not scale and mostly invents geography. This does neither: the Nilgiri Canopy is in the Nilgiri, the Narmada University Library is on the Narmada field map, and saying so is a fact canon already holds. The atlas resolves a position from the parent and **draws it as inherited rather than surveyed** -- a hollow marker, not a filled one -- so the map never claims a precision it does not have.

A place with its own `coordinates` ignores this. A place with neither is simply unplaced, which stays honest and common.

epochs.description: Epoch ids from database/timeline/epochs.json. Absent means the place exists in every era.

states.description:
What changed, and when, for the few places that genuinely transform.

A place states its identity once and overrides only what moved. Most places carry no states at all and are eight-line files; this exists for the handful like Dwarka, a working harbour in Civilization Dawn and a drowned gate after the Shattering.

Usually what changes is a name or a status, not a position -- a city does not move. The exception is the Shattering itself, which fractured the world along tectonic and dimensional boundaries at once, so `coordinates` may be restated here for somewhere it carried with it.

One entity per place per epoch was the alternative and was rejected: it multiplies hundreds by six and makes 'is this the same place?' unanswerable.

name.description: What it is called in this era, if that changed.

coordinates.description:
Where the place sits in this era, if the Shattering moved it.

Unused, and likely to stay that way. The Great Shattering is withheld on purpose -- canon keeps its consequences and not its account, because working it out is what the player is there to do. So there is no statement of what moved or how far, and there is not going to be one in `events`.

The field remains because it is the honest shape: a city does not move, but a continent that fractures takes its cities with it. If the drip through `discoveries` ever establishes where something stood before, this is where that goes.

status.description: A short state word -- drowned, ruined, founded, abandoned, buried.

held_by.description: The faction that held this place in the era, when the era's map says. The Age of Machinery chart colours places by nation; this is that colour as a fact.

confirmed.description: False where the era's chart marks the place with '?': placed, but not yet settled.
